newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN refugee body asks access to Burmese Moslems.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee body asks access to Burmese Moslems.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Friday it was appealing to the Bangladesh government to give it access to thousands of of Burmese Moslems who have fled across the border over the past two months.

Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole told reporters many of the estimated 7,000 new refugees -- whom Bangladesh regards as economic migrants -- were being jailed or forcibly returned to Burma which some of them say they fled for political reasons.
"We are not being given access to these people," she said. "We wrote to the Bangladesh government two weeks ago asking to be given access to them but so far have received no reply.

"We believe some of them may genuinely fear persecution if they return to Myanmar (Burma). We again call on the Balngladesh government to allow us to interview these people and establish who might be deserving of UNHCR protection."

O'Toole said many of the latest arrivals had cited purely economic reasons -- such as a recent surge in the price of rice in Burma -- for moving across the border, which was quite common at this time of year.
But some had told journalists they were fleeing "because of excessive forced labour, and some have even alleged that they have been tortured," she added.
The new arrivals of Burmese Moslems, known as Rohinga, are the latest to move into Bangladesh since some 250,000 crossed the border in the early 1990s.

Most of those have since been repatriated under programmes the UNHCR has agreed with the Burmese and Bangladesh governments, but some 21,000 were left -- 7,500 of whom have been cleared for return by the authorities in Rangoon.

O'Toole told a news briefing the Geneva-based UNHCR had been calling on the Bangladesh government to allow the remainder to stay, although the government in Dacca recently told the agency that it wanted them all to return.

"Quite apart from the problem that many are not cleared by the Myanmar authorities as genuine Myanmar citizens, we believe that a proportion of the remaining refugees may also risk persecution if they return home," she said.

Bangladesh had shown great hospitality to the 250,000, who began fleeing Burma in 1991. "We again appeal to the Bangladesh government to show flexibility in their treatment of the final caseload," the UNHCR spokeswoman added.

The London-based Amnesty International said in its latest annual report that 1996 was the worst year for human rights in Burma since 1990. More than 2,000 people were arrested for calling for human rights reforms and opposition figures were attacked by organised mobs, it said.
